claim: A 3.3 MDa macromolecular cage is formed between the hexameric AAA+ ATPase RavA and the decameric inducible lysine decarboxylase LdcI in E. coli.
source: A 3.3 MDa macromolecular cage between two Escherichia coli proteins with seemingly incompatible symmetries–the hexameric AAA+ ATPase RavA and the decameric inducible lysine decarboxylase LdcI–is reconstructed by cryo-electron microscopy to 11 Å resolution.
evidence: The abstract states the mass and composition of the complex, supported by the cryo-EM reconstruction presented in the manuscript.

claim: The LdcI-RavA complex was reconstructed by cryo-electron microscopy to 11 Å resolution.
source: A 3.3 MDa macromolecular cage between two Escherichia coli proteins with seemingly incompatible symmetries–the hexameric AAA+ ATPase RavA and the decameric inducible lysine decarboxylase LdcI–is reconstructed by cryo-electron microscopy to 11 Å resolution.
evidence: The resolution is stated in the abstract and supported by FSC curves in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The minimal complex between LdcI and the LdcI-binding domain of RavA was reconstructed to 7.5 Å resolution.
source: Combined with a 7.5 Å resolution reconstruction of the minimal complex between LdcI and the LdcI-binding domain of RavA, and the previously solved crystal structures of the individual components, this work enables to build a reliable pseudoatomic model of this unusual architecture and to identify conformational rearrangements and specific elements essential for complex formation.
evidence: The resolution is stated in the abstract and supported by FSC curves in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The design of the cage created via lateral interactions between five RavA rings is unique for the diverse AAA+ ATPase superfamily.
source: The design of the cage created via lateral interactions between five RavA rings is unique for the diverse AAA+ ATPase superfamily.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with other AAA+ ATPase structures in the manuscript and the statement that this is the only complex composed of several laterally interacting AAA+ ATPase rings.

claim: Members of the MoxR family of AAA+ ATPases are important modulators of multiple stress tolerance pathways.
source: Widespread among bacteria and archea, members of the MoxR family of AAA+ ATPases are important modulators of multiple stress tolerance pathways (Snider et al., 2006; Wong and Houry, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RavA has been associated with oxidative stress, antibiotic resistance and iron-sulfur cluster assembly in E. coli.
source: The best characterized MoxR representative, the RavA protein, has been recently associated to oxidative stress, antibiotic resistance and iron-sulfur cluster assembly in Escherichia coli (Babu et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RavA is involved in acid stress and nutrient stress responses via its interaction with LdcI.
source: Furthermore, it is involved in acid stress and nutrient stress responses via its interaction with the acid stress-inducible lysine decarboxylase LdcI, which buffers the bacterial cytoplasm by transforming lysine into cadaverine while consuming intracellular protons and producing CO2 (Sabo et al., 1974; Soksawatmaekhin et al., 2004; Snider et al., 2006; Wong and Houry, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: LdcI buffers the bacterial cytoplasm by transforming lysine into cadaverine while consuming intracellular protons and producing CO2.
source: Furthermore, it is involved in acid stress and nutrient stress responses via its interaction with the acid stress-inducible lysine decarboxylase LdcI, which buffers the bacterial cytoplasm by transforming lysine into cadaverine while consuming intracellular protons and producing CO2 (Sabo et al., 1974; Soksawatmaekhin et al., 2004; Snider et al., 2006; Wong and Houry, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature describing LdcI function.

claim: RavA prevents binding of LdcI to its potent inhibitor, the stringent response alarmone ppGpp.
source: We recently demonstrated that RavA prevented binding of LdcI to its potent inhibitor, the stringent response alarmone, ppGpp (El Bakkouri et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The LdcI–RavA complex maintains LdcI activity even if the bacterium experiences both acid stress and starvation.
source: Thus the LdcI–RavA complex maintains LdcI activity even if the bacterium experiences both acid stress and starvation, as it is often the case in the host stomach through which enterobacteria transit before reaching the bowel where the pathogenesis typically occurs (El Bakkouri et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and logical inference from the mechanism of RavA preventing ppGpp binding.

claim: RavA is a 300 kDa lily-shaped hexameric ring.
source: Indeed, RavA is a 300 kDa lily-shaped hexameric ring (El Bakkouri et al., 2010), whereas LdcI is a 800 kDa toroid composed of two pentameric rings stacked together back-to-back (Kanjee et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous crystal structure study.

claim: LdcI is a 800 kDa toroid composed of two pentameric rings stacked together back-to-back.
source: Indeed, RavA is a 300 kDa lily-shaped hexameric ring (El Bakkouri et al., 2010), whereas LdcI is a 800 kDa toroid composed of two pentameric rings stacked together back-to-back (Kanjee et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous crystal structure study.

claim: The strength of the interaction between RavA and LdcI has a Kd of about 20 nM.
source: The strength of the interaction (Kd of about 20 nM) between these two symmetry mismatched proteins and the resulting mass of 3.3 MDa inferred from analytical ultracentrifugation came out as a surprise (Snider et al., 2006; El Bakkouri et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous biochemical studies.

claim: The foot of RavA, called LARA, is necessary and sufficient for LdcI binding, albeit with a three orders of magnitude lower affinity than the full-length RavA.
source: We biochemically showed that the foot of RavA, inserted into the discontinuous triple helical bundle protruding as a leg from the AAA+ ATPase core, is necessary and sufficient for LdcI binding, albeit with a three orders of magnitude lower affinity. We therefore called this foot domain LARA for 'LdcI associating domain of RavA' (El Bakkouri et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous biochemical studies by the authors.

claim: The LdcI–RavA assembly features two parallel five-petal blossoms of LdcI festooned by a garland of five RavA lilies.
source: The astounding LdcI–RavA assembly is reminiscent of a symmetrical floral pattern, featuring two parallel five-petal blossoms of LdcI festooned by a garland of five RavA lilies.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM reconstruction and pseudoatomic model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The entire LdcI–RavA complex possesses dihedral fivefold symmetry.
source: The entire complex possesses the dihedral fivefold symmetry of the lysine decarboxylase and a large central cavity of 3 × 106 Å3 (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2; Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM reconstruction shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: The LdcI–RavA complex has a large central cavity of 3 × 10^6 Å^3.
source: The entire complex possesses the dihedral fivefold symmetry of the lysine decarboxylase and a large central cavity of 3 × 106 Å3 (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2; Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM reconstruction and measurements from the structure.

claim: Upon complex formation, the RavA hexamer loses its sixfold circular symmetry.
source: Upon complex formation, the RavA hexamer loses its sixfold circular symmetry.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the RavA structure in the complex versus the isolated form, shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The compact outward-pointing hub formed by the six AAA+ modules of RavA remains virtually unchanged upon complex formation.
source: The compact outward-pointing hub formed by the six AAA+ modules remains virtually unchanged and the ATP binding sites preserved, whereas the legs massively rearrange in order to comply with the dihedral symmetry of the whole assembly (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ATP binding sites of RavA are preserved upon complex formation with LdcI.
source: The compact outward-pointing hub formed by the six AAA+ modules remains virtually unchanged and the ATP binding sites preserved, whereas the legs massively rearrange in order to comply with the dihedral symmetry of the whole assembly (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The legs of RavA massively rearrange upon complex formation to comply with the dihedral symmetry of the assembly.
source: The compact outward-pointing hub formed by the six AAA+ modules remains virtually unchanged and the ATP binding sites preserved, whereas the legs massively rearrange in order to comply with the dihedral symmetry of the whole assembly (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Four protomers of each of the five RavA hexamers are involved in the interaction with LdcI.
source: Four protomers of each of the five RavA hexamers are involved in the interaction with the LdcI, while the remaining two legs of each hexamer mediate the RavA–RavA interaction at the equator of the complex (Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis and pseudoatomic model shown in the figures and videos.

claim: The remaining two legs of each RavA hexamer mediate the RavA–RavA interaction at the equator of the complex.
source: Four protomers of each of the five RavA hexamers are involved in the interaction with the LdcI, while the remaining two legs of each hexamer mediate the RavA–RavA interaction at the equator of the complex (Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in the figures and videos.

claim: The scaffold provided by the AAA+ hub and the triple helical bundles of RavA increases the stability of the LdcI–RavA cage compared to the minimal LdcI-LARA complex.
source: Compared to the minimal LdcI-LARA complex, the scaffold provided by the AAA+ hub and the triple helical bundles of the entire RavA increases the stability of the LdcI–RavA cage.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis and comparison between the full complex and the minimal complex.

claim: The RavA hexamers morph into two axially superimposed triskelia rotated 180° with respect to each other.
source: Specifically, the RavA hexamers morph into two axially superimposed triskelia rotated 180° with respect to each other (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The triskelion configuration and the loop (amino acids 329–360) at the beginning of the LARA domain allow the optimal positioning of each LARA domain for interaction with LdcI subunits.
source: The triskelion configuration and the loop (amino acids 329–360) at the beginning of the LARA domain allow the optimal positioning of each LARA domain for interaction with LdcI subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and mutational studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the LdcI–RavA complex, one ring of each LdcI faces the exterior of the complex, while the second faces the cavity.
source: Indeed, in the context of the complex, the two rings of each LdcI particle are not placed equivalently—one ring of each LdcI faces the exterior of the complex, while the second faces the cavity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in the figures.

claim: One leg of the RavA triskelion stretches its foot out to present the LARA domain to the subunits of the inner ring of LdcI from above.
source: Remarkably, one leg of the RavA triskelion stretches its foot out in order to present the LARA domain to the subunits of the inner ring of LdcI from above, while in the second leg the N-terminus of the loop sharply bends, allowing the foot to interact with the outer ring of LdcI from underneath (Figure 1B, Figure 2B,C,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in the figures.

claim: In the second leg of the RavA triskelion, the N-terminus of the loop sharply bends, allowing the foot to interact with the outer ring of LdcI from underneath.
source: Remarkably, one leg of the RavA triskelion stretches its foot out in order to present the LARA domain to the subunits of the inner ring of LdcI from above, while in the second leg the N-terminus of the loop sharply bends, allowing the foot to interact with the outer ring of LdcI from underneath (Figure 1B, Figure 2B,C,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Both feet of RavA appear to interact with the inner or the outer rings of LdcI in exactly the same way.
source: As a result of these intricate rotations, both feet appear to interact with the inner or the outer rings of LdcI in exactly the same way.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and comparison with the LdcI-LARA complex.

claim: In the LdcI-LARA complex, each LdcI protomer binds one LARA domain.
source: This surprising finding is confirmed by the 7.5 Å resolution cryoEM map of the LdcI-LARA complex where each LdcI protomer binds one LARA domain, and which can be perfectly superimposed with the 3D reconstruction of the entire LdcI–RavA complex (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM reconstruction shown in Figure 2D and supplementary figures.

claim: The LdcI-LARA complex structure can be perfectly superimposed with the 3D reconstruction of the entire LdcI–RavA complex.
source: This surprising finding is confirmed by the 7.5 Å resolution cryoEM map of the LdcI-LARA complex where each LdcI protomer binds one LARA domain, and which can be perfectly superimposed with the 3D reconstruction of the entire LdcI–RavA complex (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: At 7.5 Å resolution, the crystal structures of LdcI and LARA can be docked into the EM density unambiguously because the secondary structure elements are clearly resolved.
source: At this resolution, the crystal structures of LdcI and LARA can be docked into the EM density unambiguously because the secondary structure elements are clearly resolved (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quality of the cryo-EM map shown in the figures.

claim: The LdcI decamer is barely affected by the LARA domain binding.
source: The LdcI decamer can be considered as barely affected by the LARA domain binding and all LdcI-LARA interaction sites are indeed equivalent (Figure 2E,F, Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in the figures.

claim: All LdcI-LARA interaction sites are equivalent.
source: The LdcI decamer can be considered as barely affected by the LARA domain binding and all LdcI-LARA interaction sites are indeed equivalent (Figure 2E,F, Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The loop 329–360 of RavA is responsible for the LdcI-LARA interaction.
source: Noteworthy, it is the loop 329–360 of RavA which is responsible for the LdcI-LARA interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and mutational studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Two legs of each RavA triskelion place the LARA domains on the LdcI.
source: Two legs of each triskelion place the LARA domains on the LdcI.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The third legs of each RavA triskelion interact laterally with their counterparts from the neighboring RavA via their triple helical bundles.
source: The third legs interact laterally with their counterparts from the neighboring RavA via their triple helical bundles while the above-mentioned loop 329–360 of their LARA domain feet packs against the triple helical domain of a neighboring RavA hexamer, further stabilizing the complex architecture (Figure 1B, Figure 2B,C,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The loop 329–360 of the LARA domain feet packs against the triple helical domain of a neighboring RavA hexamer, further stabilizing the complex architecture.
source: The third legs interact laterally with their counterparts from the neighboring RavA via their triple helical bundles while the above-mentioned loop 329–360 of their LARA domain feet packs against the triple helical domain of a neighboring RavA hexamer, further stabilizing the complex architecture (Figure 1B, Figure 2B,C,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Critical residues in LdcI required for RavA binding are E634 and Y697, both part of a C-terminal β-sheet.
source: Thus, critical residues in LdcI required for RavA binding were found to be E634 and Y697, both part of a C-terminal β-sheet (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The charged residues R347 and R348 and the hydrophobic residues I343 and F344 at the tip of the LARA domain loop are required for RavA binding to LdcI.
source: The charged residues R347 and R348 and the hydrophobic residues I343 and F344 at the tip of the LARA domain loop are required for RavA binding to LdcI (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The interaction between RavA and LdcI is mediated both by charged and hydrophobic residues.
source: Hence, the data suggest that the interaction between the two proteins is mediated both by charged and hydrophobic residues.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutational analysis results.

claim: Shortening the loop 329–360 by deleting residues 329–335 weakens or abolishes the LdcI–RavA complex formation.
source: Moreover, shortening the loop by deleting residues 329–335, or constraining its N-terminus by introducting two prolines (S331P, D332P), weakens or abolishes the LdcI–RavA complex formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Constraining the N-terminus of the loop 329–360 by introducing two prolines (S331P, D332P) weakens or abolishes the LdcI–RavA complex formation.
source: Moreover, shortening the loop by deleting residues 329–335, or constraining its N-terminus by introducting two prolines (S331P, D332P), weakens or abolishes the LdcI–RavA complex formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Mutating residues R315 and E452 in the first and second helices of the RavA triple helical bundle destabilized complex formation.
source: Finally, mutating residues R315 and E452 in the first and second helices of the RavA triple helical bundle, respectively, destabilized complex formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,E,F) suggesting that the RavA–RavA leg–leg interaction is mediated by these two helices.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The RavA–RavA leg–leg interaction is mediated by the first and second helices of the triple helical bundle.
source: Finally, mutating residues R315 and E452 in the first and second helices of the RavA triple helical bundle, respectively, destabilized complex formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,E,F) suggesting that the RavA–RavA leg–leg interaction is mediated by these two helices.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutational analysis results.

claim: The loop at the N-terminus of the LARA domain is involved in positioning the foot in respect to the rest of the leg to allow for equivalent interaction with both the inner and the outer LdcI rings.
source: To summarize, the same loop at the N-terminus of the LARA domain appears involved in (1) positioning the foot in respect to the rest of the leg so that to allow for equivalent interaction with both the inner and the outer LdcI rings, (2) binding to LdcI, and (3) binding to the triple helical bundle of the adjacent RavA (Figure 2B,E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and mutational studies.

claim: The loop at the N-terminus of the LARA domain is involved in binding to LdcI.
source: To summarize, the same loop at the N-terminus of the LARA domain appears involved in (1) positioning the foot in respect to the rest of the leg so that to allow for equivalent interaction with both the inner and the outer LdcI rings, (2) binding to LdcI, and (3) binding to the triple helical bundle of the adjacent RavA (Figure 2B,E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and mutational studies.

claim: The loop at the N-terminus of the LARA domain is involved in binding to the triple helical bundle of the adjacent RavA.
source: To summarize, the same loop at the N-terminus of the LARA domain appears involved in (1) positioning the foot in respect to the rest of the leg so that to allow for equivalent interaction with both the inner and the outer LdcI rings, (2) binding to LdcI, and (3) binding to the triple helical bundle of the adjacent RavA (Figure 2B,E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and mutational studies.

claim: The loop 329–360 of the LARA domain clearly emerges as the main determinant of the LdcI–RavA cage formation.
source: This loop therefore clearly emerges as the main determinant of the LdcI–RavA cage formation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structural and mutational analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The structural plasticity of the loop 329–360 is essential to fulfill its role in complex formation.
source: While the 7.5 Å resolution of the current LdcI-LARA reconstruction precludes building a reliable pseudoatomic model of the 329–360 LARA domain loop based on the experimental EM density, its structural plasticity is obviously essential to fullful this role (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structural analysis and mutational studies.

claim: The LdcI–RavA complex architecture has certain principles in common with eukaryotic vesicle coats, particularly clathrin coats.
source: The fact that LdcI–RavA complex and eukaryotic vesicle coats have certain architectural principles in common is striking, because the LdcI–RavA architecture is remarkably different from all AAA+ ATPase assemblies described so far.
evidence: This claim is based on structural comparison and analogy discussed in the manuscript.

claim: The LdcI–RavA architecture is the only complex composed of several laterally interacting AAA+ ATPase rings out of 30 released EM maps in EMDB and 43 oligomeric crystal structures in PDB as of July 2014.
source: Indeed, to our knowledge it is the only complex (out of 30 released EM maps in EMDB and 43 oligomeric crystal structures in PDB in July 2014) composed of several laterally interacting AAA+ ATPase rings, and the only one enclosing a central cavity other than the cavity framed by the AAA+ modules assembled into a ring or a spiral.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with known structures in databases.

claim: The LdcI–RavA complex is the only AAA+ ATPase assembly enclosing a central cavity other than the cavity framed by the AAA+ modules assembled into a ring or a spiral.
source: Indeed, to our knowledge it is the only complex (out of 30 released EM maps in EMDB and 43 oligomeric crystal structures in PDB in July 2014) composed of several laterally interacting AAA+ ATPase rings, and the only one enclosing a central cavity other than the cavity framed by the AAA+ modules assembled into a ring or a spiral.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with known structures in databases.

claim: The scaffold provided by the AAA+ hub and the triple helical legs of RavA is required to glue the LARA domain in place and effectively preclude ppGpp binding.
source: One may posit an explanation based on the markedly higher stability of the entire LdcI–RavA complex compared to the LdcI-LARA complex: the scaffold provided by the AAA+ hub and the triple helical legs of RavA is required to glue the LARA domain in place and effectively preclude ppGpp binding.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the structural observations.

claim: The LARA foot binds approximately 30 Å away from the closest ppGpp binding pocket.
source: Noteworthy, the LARA foot binds ∼30 Å away from the closest ppGpp binding pocket.
evidence: This claim is based on measurements from the structural model.

claim: The LARA domain does not appear to directly block the access of ppGpp to its binding pocket but rather to induce a local conformational change in this pocket reducing ppGpp affinity.
source: Thus, contrary to our earlier prediction based on the low resolution negative stain EM map (Snider et al., 2006; El Bakkouri et al., 2010), the LARA domain does not appear to directly block the access of ppGpp to its binding pocket but rather to induce a local conformational change in this pocket reducing ppGpp affinity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structural analysis and distance measurements.

claim: RavA and its binding partner ViaA are involved in Fe–S cluster assembly and particular respiratory pathways.
source: Along these lines, an involvement of RavA and its binding partner, a VWA-domain protein ViaA, in the Fe–S cluster assembly and particular respiratory pathways (Babu et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2014) and a physical interaction of RavA, ViaA (Wong et al., 2014) and LdcI (Erhardt et al., 2012) with specific subunits of the highly conserved respiratory complex I (Erhardt et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2014) were recently documented.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: RavA, ViaA, and LdcI physically interact with specific subunits of the highly conserved respiratory complex I.
source: Along these lines, an involvement of RavA and its binding partner, a VWA-domain protein ViaA, in the Fe–S cluster assembly and particular respiratory pathways (Babu et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2014) and a physical interaction of RavA, ViaA (Wong et al., 2014) and LdcI (Erhardt et al., 2012) with specific subunits of the highly conserved respiratory complex I (Erhardt et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2014) were recently documented.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: The LdcI–RavA cage may act as a chaperone, protecting substrates from denaturation or disassembly under acid stress conditions inside the central cavity.
source: Our structure of the exquisite LdcI–RavA cage substantiates a hypothesis that it may act as a chaperone, protecting substrates from denaturation or disassembly under acid stress conditions inside the central cavity, and spurs on further functional investigation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the structural features and known functions of MoxR proteins.

claim: The resolution of the LdcI–RavA complex based on the unmasked FSC curve was 14 Å.
source: The resolution estimated based on the unmasked FSC curve was 14 Å, whereas the FSC curve obtained with soft shaped masks (dilated 5 pixels and with a fall–off profile of a cosine half-bell of 4 pixel width) yielded the resolution of 11 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the FSC curves shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The resolution of the LdcI-LARA complex based on the unmasked FSC curve was 8.8 Å.
source: The resolution estimated based on the unmasked FSC curve was 8.8 Å, whereas the FSC curve obtained with soft shaped masks (dilated 5 pixels and with a fall–off profile of a cosine half-bell of 4 pixel width) yielded the resolution of 7.5 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the FSC curves shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The final 3D reconstruction of the LdcI–RavA complex comprised 21,265 particles.
source: The final map comprised 21,265 particles with an even view distribution around the equatorial axis.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the data processing.

claim: The final 3D reconstruction of the LdcI-LARA complex comprised 23,540 particles.
source: The final 3D reconstruction comprised 23,540 particles.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the data processing.

claim: The Cα RMSD between the initial pdb of the LdcI monomer model and the final Flex-EM model is 0.65 Å.
source: The Cα RMSD between the initial pdb of the LdcI monomer model and the final Flex-EM model is 0.65 Å.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the fitting procedure.

claim: The cross correlation value between the LdcI-LARA cryoEM map and the rigidly fitted LdcI monomer is 0.75.
source: The cross correlation values between the cryoEM map and either the rigidly fitted monomer or the final Flex-EM model are 0.75 and 0.84 respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the fitting procedure.

claim: The cross correlation value between the LdcI-LARA cryoEM map and the final Flex-EM model of LdcI is 0.84.
source: The cross correlation values between the cryoEM map and either the rigidly fitted monomer or the final Flex-EM model are 0.75 and 0.84 respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the fitting procedure.

claim: The cross-correlation between the LdcI–RavA and LdcI-LARA maps filtered at 11 Å resolution is 0.86.
source: For LdcI–RavA fitting, superposition of LdcI–RavA and LdcI-LARA maps (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C), demonstrated that LdcI and LARA positions were conserved in both maps (cross-correlation of 0.86 between the two maps filtered at 11 Å resolution).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the fitting procedure.

claim: CryoEM maps and Cα traces of the corresponding fitted atomic structures have been deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank and Protein Data Bank with accession codes EMD-2679 and PDB-4upb for LdcI–RavA.
source: CryoEM maps and Cα traces of the corresponding fitted atomic structures have been deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank and Protein Data Bank, respectively, with accession codes EMD-2679 and PDB-4upb for LdcI–RavA, EMD-2681 and PDB-4upf for LdcI-LARA.
evidence: This is stated in the Accession codes section.

claim: CryoEM maps and Cα traces of the corresponding fitted atomic structures have been deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank and Protein Data Bank with accession codes EMD-2681 and PDB-4upf for LdcI-LARA.
source: CryoEM maps and Cα traces of the corresponding fitted atomic structures have been deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank and Protein Data Bank, respectively, with accession codes EMD-2679 and PDB-4upb for LdcI–RavA, EMD-2681 and PDB-4upf for LdcI-LARA.
evidence: This is stated in the Accession codes section.
